Nothing in this file would exfiltrate data, download executable payloads, or run attacker-controlled commands at parse time.

LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
 <security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard Arch `-bin` PKGBUILD that repackages the upstream `httm` project's own release artifact. The single source is downloaded over HTTPS from the project's official GitHub releases URL and pinned with a concrete SHA-512 checksum (not `SKIP`), so the `.deb` is verified before any extraction. `prepare()` extracts `data.tar.xz` from the `.deb` and decompresses the man page; `package()` installs the `httm` binary and its upstream companion helpers `bowie`, `ounce`, and `nicotine` (renamed `httm-nicotine` to avoid a clash with the unrelated Nicotine+ player) into `$pkgdir`. Those helpers are part of the checksum-verified upstream `.deb`, not code injected by the AUR maintainer. The `command -v zfs` conditionals are a normal runtime-dependency check deciding whether to install the ZFS-specific `ounce` helper and are harmless.

I found no obfuscation, no `eval`/`base64`/`curl|bash` or other download-and-execute patterns, no unexpected network access, no writes outside `$pkgdir`, and no `git pull`/`fetch`/`reset` at build time. The only oddities are cosmetic: the character-class substitution `${pkgname//[-bin]/}` (which happens to reduce `httm-bin` to `httm`) and a redundant `exit 0` inside the `command -v zfs` command substitutions. Neither changes the script's behavior in any dangerous way. The only caveat is functional rather than security-related: if the installed `makepkg` version does not automatically extract `.deb` archives, the build would fail in `prepare()`; that would be a packaging defect, not evidence of malice.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Safe standard httm-bin repackage: verified upstream .deb, no malicious behavior.</summary>
</security_assessment>
